newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian refiners look West for cheaper crude oil.
newsitem.headline: Asian refiners look West for cheaper crude oil.

text.p: Asia's traditional crude oil suppliers are facing increased competition from western cargoes as price-conscious Asian refiners looked further afield for cheaper oil, traders said on Tuesday.
They said it was becoming increasingly common for West African crudes to arrive to Asia since last year, but this trend would only last as long as those crudes remained cheaper.

Cargoes from Egypt, the North Sea and South America, priced against the global benchmark crudes Brent or West Texas Intermediate (WTI), are also gaining popularity, finding new buyers in Japan and South Korea.
In August, more than 650,000 barrels per day (bpd) of spot crudes are due to arrive in Asia from West and North Africa and other western countries.
Between January and May this year, London tanker broker Simpson, Spence and Young estimated that 805,000 bpd of West African crudes headed to Asia.
Traders said buyers found western grades cheaper compared with Asian and Middle Eastern grades, which are their traditional supply sources.

South Korean refiners also saw a pressing need to diversify their supply sources because they have significantly raised their crude processing capacity to about 1.2 million barrels per day (bpd) since last year.

South Korean refiner Hyundai Oil Refinery Co, an affiliate of Hyundai Group HYGR.CN, bought its first cargo of Egyptian Gulf of Suez crude early this month, attracted by the lower price of Brent-related crudes.
Low Brent values also prompted Japan's Cosmo Oil Co Ltd to buy its first Gulf of Suez cargo in seven years.
The Gulf of Suez crude has been sold to Asia before, but mainly by monthly spot tenders to India, and only sporadically moved to Northeast Asia.
"Middle East crudes are quite cheap, since Oman and Abu Dhabi crudes are at discounts," a Hyundai source told Reuters. "But the Gulf of Suez priced against Brent is still cheaper."
Another South Korean refiner, Ssangyong Oil also bought its first West African crude cargo early this month.

Ssangyong purchased the two-million-barrel cargo of Nigeria's Bonny Light to meet the country's stringent fuel oil specifications, but the crude was also comparatively cheaper than Asian light sweet crudes of the same grade, traders said. Norway's Oseberg crude and Argentina's Escalante crude were also sold to Chinese refiners earlier this month, which were probably only the second cargoes of each grades sold to China.

The main attraction of these crudes is that they are priced against the WTI and Brent, traders said. The recent weakness in the Brent and WTI prices have narrowed the price differential between Dubai and the western benchmark crudes, making the western grades cheaper.
In early June, the front month price of Brent on London's International Petroleum Exchange hit a 13-month low of $17.38, before recovering to the current $17.98.

Despite the current crave for western crudes, traders remained uncertain if the western crudes would come to Asia on a regular basis, as their attraction was determined by the Brent/Dubai spread or the difference between the benchmark crudes.
When these cargoes were sold to Asian refiners in early June the Brent/Dubai spread has narrowed to 50 cents a barrel, from $1.00 in May.

"It will depend on how the Middle East prices react, and if the Middle East official prices will fall low enough to widen the Brent/Dubai spread, thus making Middle East grades more competitive" said a trader with a major oil company.
